notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Amos 3 from the sources retrieved.

---

## Amos 3 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

Amos 3–6 form a connected series, expanding the indictment and sentence of Amos 2:6–16. The chapter opens the first of three main addresses (each beginning “Hear this word”: 3:1, 4:1, 5:1). God’s special relationship with Israel — proved by the Exodus — makes their sin and coming judgment all the more serious. Amos then defends his prophetic authority through a chain of seven rhetorical questions (vv. 3–6) that build to the conclusion that God Himself is behind the coming calamity. The chapter closes with a summons to pagan nations to witness Israel’s corruption and the coming destruction of Samaria’s altars and luxury houses.

— Pulpit Commentary (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)  
— Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

### v. 1 — “Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt”

- The summons is to all twelve tribes (“the whole family”), though the denunciation that follows is aimed chiefly at the northern kingdom of Israel. Judah is only indirectly warned. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott notes that “children of Israel” (rather than “house of Israel”) is less usual in Amos, and the phrase “whole family” signals that both kingdoms are addressed, though the Ten Tribes are chiefly in view. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- The reference to the Exodus (“brought up from the land of Egypt”) is the crowning act of God’s favour, and it makes Israel’s rejection of God doubly inexcusable. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Gill observes that Israel was a “family under the peculiar care of Jehovah” and the Exodus was the foundation of all subsequent blessings; therefore God had every right to chastise them. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 2 — “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.”

- “Known” here means loved, chosen, acknowledged — not mere intellectual awareness. It speaks of covenant intimacy (cf. Hosea 13:5; Nahum 1:7). (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- God makes a clear connection between privilege and responsibility: being chosen does not mean immunity from judgment; it means greater accountability. As G. Campbell Morgan put it, “The measure of our privilege, in the Divine economy, is the measure of our responsibility.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- Gill adds that Israel’s sins were “more aggravated than others, being against goodness and mercy, light and knowledge,” and therefore deserving of more stripes (cf. Luke 12:47; 1 Peter 4:17). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that unlike the pagan nations denounced in Amos 1–2, Israel had “sinned against light and knowledge and love,” so her sentence must be heavier. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 3 — “Can two walk together without agreeing where to go?”

- **Traditional reading (Pulpit, Ellicott):** The “two” are God and the prophet — i.e., God’s judgment and the prophet’s word do not coincide by chance. The prophet announces judgment because God has commissioned him; there is prior agreement. The application is seen in vv. 7–8. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- **Alternative traditional reading (Gill, many devotional writers):** The “two” are God and Israel. There can be no fellowship or communion between God and His people if they are not in harmony — if they are walking contrary to Him. Sin breaks the walk. Gill expands this into a full spiritual application: reconciliation through Christ, the Spirit slaying enmity, and the believer walking with God in faith and ordinances. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- **Reformed / Calvin:** Calvin sees the verse as part of Amos’s defence of his prophetic authority, not as a general statement about human relationships. (Calvin excerpts at CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol27/htm/iv.iii.ii.htm)
- Spurgeon preached on this verse, applying it to the necessity of agreement between Christ and the believer for a walk of fellowship. (Precept Austin Spurgeon page: https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_sermons_on_amos)

---

### v. 4 — “Does a lion roar in the forest when he has no prey? Does a young lion growl in his den if he has caught nothing?”

- The lion roars when prey is in sight and he is about to spring. So God makes the prophet utter his voice because He is ready to execute vengeance. The young lion (*kephir*) growls over prey already in the lair — Israel lies helpless as God’s threatenings strike. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott similarly: the questions suggest the prey is *being seized right now*. The lion’s roar and the young lion’s growl signal that nations and this family of Israel are already “trembling in the grasp of the great Avenger.” (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- Gill notes the natural observation: a lion does not roar unless it has prey in sight or in its paws. He links this back to Amos 1:2 (“The LORD will roar from Zion”) — prophecy in a way of judgment never comes without cause; sin makes a people the prey of divine wrath. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word treats this as the second in a chain of six “obviously true” statements, each building toward v. 6b: when calamity comes, the LORD has done it. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

### v. 5 — “Does a bird land in a snare where no bait has been set? Does a trap spring from the ground when it has nothing to catch?”

- The thought is that punishment is both *deserved* and *certain*. A bird is not caught unless a trap is set; the trap the sinner sets for himself is sin. The second clause means: a snare does not spring up from the ground without having caught something. When God appoints retributive punishment, it comes with absolute certainty. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott renders the second clause: “Does the snare rise up from the ground, and take nothing at all?” (correcting the KJV “take up”). The idea is that Israel, “like a silly dove,” is falling into snares, and the armies that will enclose Israel are already in motion. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- Gill observes that no judgment or affliction comes by chance; God’s nets and snares are set on purpose. Moreover, God does not remove the snare (affliction) until its end is answered — whether bringing men to repentance or removing sin. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 6 — “If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble? If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?”

- The trumpet (*shofar*) is the alarm of war. Just as its sound naturally produces fear, so the prophet’s denunciation should arouse alarm. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- **On “calamity” / “evil”:** The “evil” here is *malum poenae* — the evil of affliction or calamity, not moral evil (*malum culpae*). As Augustine said: “Evil which is sin the Lord hath not done; evil which is punishment for sin the Lord bringeth.” (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- All phenomena are ascribed in the Bible to divine operation; no second causes are allowed to interfere. This does not make God the author of sin, but the sovereign Lord over all calamity used as judgment. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- **Reformed emphasis:** This verse is a key proof-text for divine sovereignty over all events, including disasters. John Piper cites it alongside Lamentations 3:37 and Proverbs 16:33 to argue that nothing — not even calamity — happens apart from God’s sovereign will. (Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/treasuring-christ-and-the-call-to-suffer-part-3; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/where-is-god--2)
- Enduring Word: When judgment comes, everyone should know “it won’t be an accident, fate, or bad luck. It will be the hand of the Lord.” This is the climactic seventh statement the six previous questions build toward. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- Gill also notes the alternate marginal reading: “and shall not the Lord do somewhat?” — i.e., if sin runs rampant, will not God arise and act? (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 7 — “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.”

- **Traditional reading:** In context, this refers specifically to coming *judgment* upon Israel. God revealed this “secret” (*sod*) to His prophets beforehand so that Israel would have every opportunity to repent and no excuse for being surprised. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/; Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- **Calvin’s crucial qualification (Reformed view):** Calvin insists this verse “ought to be confined to that people [Israel], and it ought also to be confined to the punishments of which the Prophet speaks.” God deals with His covenant people differently than with heathen nations — He warns them beforehand. Calvin explicitly rejects the idea that this verse “impose[s] a necessity on God, as if he was not free to do any thing without previously revealing it.” God executes many judgments hidden from both men and angels. The point is to condemn Israel’s obstinacy: they were warned and still refused to repent. (Calvin, via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-3.html; also at CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol27/htm/iv.iii.ii.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** The imagery of vv. 3–8 indicates Amos had a message so true and sure that he had to proclaim it; God knew how Israel would respond, but that does not remove the force of the warning nor the need to repent. (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servants-prophets)
- Gill broadens the application: God revealed the flood to Noah, Sodom’s destruction to Abraham, the captivity to Jeremiah, the four monarchies to Daniel, and the grand scheme of salvation through Christ “by the mouth of all the prophets from the beginning of the world.” (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word cautions that this does *not* mean God announces everything in advance; in Ephesians 3:5 Paul says God deliberately hid the nature of the church from Old Testament prophets. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

### v. 8 — “The lion has roared — who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken — who will not prophesy?”

- Amos is essentially saying, “Don’t blame me. I’m only the messenger.” As natural as it is to fear when a lion roars, that is how natural it is for the prophet to prophesy when the Lord GOD has spoken. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- The Pulpit Commentary compares this to Jeremiah 20:9 (the word like fire in his bones) and 1 Corinthians 9:16 (“necessity is laid upon me; woe to me if I do not preach the gospel”). The divine call compels the prophet to speak. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Gill draws from Amos’s own experience as a herdsman in the wilderness of Tekoa, who would have often heard a lion roar and been put in a panic. The figure is then explained: “The Lord GOD has spoken — who can but prophesy?” It is dangerous to refuse: “if the roaring of a lion is so terrible… much more the wrath and displeasure of the King of kings.” (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- Calvin connects this directly to v. 7: the prophetic compulsion is not arbitrary but arises from God’s prior revelation of His secret. (Calvin, CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol27/htm/iv.iii.ii.htm)

---

### v. 9 — “Proclaim to the citadels of Ashdod and to the citadels of Egypt: ‘Assemble on the mountains of Samaria; see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst.’”

- God summons pagan nations — Philistia (represented by Ashdod) and Egypt — as witnesses against Israel. These were Israel’s historic enemies, making the summons particularly humiliating. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that these two nations had seen God’s mighty works for Israel and could therefore appreciate her ingratitude. The mountains surrounding Samaria formed a natural amphitheatre from which spectators could look down into the city streets and observe the iniquities. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott renders “in the palaces” as “*on* the palaces” — i.e., on their flat roofs, so the message would be heard far and wide. The marginal reading “oppressions” (plural) is preferred, as the parallelism shows. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- Hubbard (cited in Enduring Word) notes that summoning Egyptians and Philistines — whose “reputations for injustice and brutality would be resented by the Israelites” — shows that “by any standards of international decency they have become culprits.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- Gill: These heathen witnesses are called to “sit in judgment” and declare whether Israel’s punishment is just. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 10 — “For they know not how to do right,’ declares the LORD. ‘They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.’”

- “They know not to do right” does not mean mere ignorance; it indicates a lost moral sense — they have become *indifferent* to right and wrong. Ellicott calls it “the awful state of utter moral impotence, wherein not only the intellectual consciousness, but the impulses to action, are languid or even paralysed — a dead conscience!” (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary says Israel “lost all sense of justice, the foundation of social life” (cf. Jeremiah 4:22). (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Gill notes this refers particularly to judges and civil magistrates who “knew what was right in the theory, but not in the practice; bribes blinded their eyes.” The riches stored in their palaces were gotten by violence and oppression. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word: “The rich and powerful of Israel used their wealth and power to oppress and steal from others.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

### v. 11 — “Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘An enemy will surround the land; he will pull down your strongholds and plunder your citadels.’”

- The “adversary” is Assyria (Shalmaneser or his successor Sargon), who invaded Israel and took Samaria less than 30 years after Amos’s prophecy (2 Kings 17). (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- The Hebrew is vivid: “an enemy and around the land” — as if the Lord already sees the foe present. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Gill: “A just retaliation” — the palaces that were “repositories of ill-gotten substance and wealth” would be plundered. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott notes “thy strength” points mainly to the stronghold of Samaria but may also include the chief warriors led away captive. The Septuagint reads “O Tyre” by mistaking the Hebrew *tsar* for *tsor*, producing a garbled rendering. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch.”

- **Traditional reading (Pulpit, Gill):** The shepherd finds only worthless remnants after the lion has devoured the sheep — “a couple of shank bones or a bit of an ear.” These scraps prove to the owner that the animal was killed by a predator (cf. Exodus 22:10–13). Likewise, only a tiny, worthless remnant of Israel will escape the coming destruction. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)
- The Pulpit Commentary notes it is unlikely the verse means a shepherd *attacks* a lion (an abnormal act of courage); the point is the shepherd finds only scraps *after* the lion has left. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word (citing Hubbard): the sarcastic point is that devastation will be so complete that all that remains as “proof of death” is scraps of furniture — “the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- **On “Damascus” / “couch”:** There is a well-known translation issue. The traditional KJV reads “in Damascus in a couch.” The Pulpit Commentary surveys the options: (1) a proper name (Damascus), meaning the Israelites trusted in Damascus for security or fled there; (2) “damask” — a silken or costly fabric for which Damascus was famous, yielding “on the silken cushions of a bed” (so Revised Version margin); (3) “a couch of Damascus” i.e., a luxurious Syrian couch. The Pulpit Commentary favours the third as easiest. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott follows Gesenius and Ewald in rendering it “on a couch’s damask,” referring to the white woollen or silken fabric from Damascus, already famous in that era. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- Gill notes that the escapees would be “poor and insignificant,” and their escape “next to a miracle.” (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 13 — “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob, declares the Lord GOD, the God of Hosts.”

- The address is to the heathen witnesses already summoned in v. 9 — they are now called to witness not only Israel’s sin but also her punishment. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- “The God of Hosts” (*Yahweh Elohei Tseva’ot*) emphasises God’s command over the powers of heaven and earth, underlining His ability to execute His threats. The Septuagint translates it *Pantokrator* (“Almighty”). (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Ellicott agrees: “Hear ye” is addressed to the foreign nations Egypt and Philistia from v. 9. (Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)

---

### v. 14 — “On the day I punish Israel for their transgressions, I will visit destruction on the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground.”

- Bethel was the northern kingdom’s national centre of idolatrous worship, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:29, 33). Though one altar is mentioned in Kings, others had likely been added. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- The “horns of the altar” were projections at the four corners on which the blood of the sin offering was smeared (Exodus 27:2; 29:12). They were considered the holiest part and symbolised the altar’s strength — as horns represent an animal’s strength. Cutting them off means the altar loses its sacred character and any supposed place of refuge. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)
- This verse echoes the earlier prophecy of 1 Kings 13:2–3 against the altar at Bethel. God will destroy the very instruments of idolatry along with the idolaters. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word: “When we build a place of idolatry, we invite God to destroy it.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

### v. 15 — “I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory will also perish, and the great houses will come to an end,” declares the LORD.

- **Winter and summer houses:** The wealthy had separate residences for different seasons — possibly different chambers within one house, or distinct royal abodes facing north or south as appropriate (cf. Judges 3:20; Jeremiah 36:22). The luxury of having both is condemned. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm; Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/amos/3.htm)
- **Houses of ivory:** Mansions panelled or inlaid with ivory, such as Ahab’s (1 Kings 22:39) and Solomon’s throne (1 Kings 10:18). The Assyrians also practiced ivory veneering. This was a mark of ostentatious wealth, often gained through oppression. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- **“Great houses”:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew more likely means “many houses” (so Septuagint, *oikoi polloi*). Not only palaces but many private houses would be destroyed (cf. Isaiah 5:9). (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/amos/3.htm)
- Enduring Word notes archaeological confirmation: eighth-century B.C. cities like Tirzah show a stark divide between large, prosperous houses and small, crowded ones — the very inequality Amos condemned. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**On vv. 3–8 (prophetic authority and divine sovereignty):**

- **Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier):** Calvin restricts v. 7 to God’s dealings with Israel concerning covenant judgment — it is not an absolute law binding God to reveal everything He does. God is free to act without prior revelation. The passage teaches that God was merciful to warn Israel through prophets, making their rejection doubly culpable. Ligonier emphasises that God’s foreknowledge of Israel’s response does not diminish the genuine offer of repentance or the prophet’s compulsion to preach. (Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/amos-3.html; Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servants-prophets)

- **Baptist (Gill, broadly Reformed Baptist):** Gill reads v. 3 as about fellowship between God and the believer — requiring agreement through Christ’s satisfaction and the Spirit’s work. He treats v. 7 more broadly than Calvin, listing many examples of God revealing His secrets (Noah, Abraham, Daniel, etc.). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/amos/3.htm)

- **Charismatic / Pentecostal:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) treats v. 7 as a general principle that God reveals coming judgment so people have time to repent, while also cautioning (from Ephesians 3:5) that this does not mean God announces *everything* in advance. Guzik’s approach is pastorally broad and does not press Calvin’s strict limitation. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/amos-3/)

- **On v. 6b and theodicy:** The Reformed tradition (Piper, Ligonier) uses Amos 3:6 as a definitive proof-text for God’s exhaustive sovereignty over disaster and calamity — all things, including catastrophes, come from the Lord’s hand and serve His purposes. Non-Reformed evangelicals often emphasise the distinction between God *permitting* and God *directly causing*, though the sources retrieved do not provide a specific Arminian/Wesleyan counter-reading within the scope of the search results. (Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/where-is-god--2)

---

**Limitations:** I was unable to retrieve dedicated commentary from Methodist/Wesleyan sources (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org), Catholic/Orthodox sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), or modern critical scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) within the search and fetch limits. The notes above are drawn from the sources that were successfully accessed.
